title: The Python Standard Library
objective: Recognize when Python's standard library already solves your problem.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.chapterTitle: Functions (Storing Functions in Modules); Classes (The Python Standard Library)
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: Python ships with a large standard library — modules that are always available once you import them, no extra installation required. Reaching for one of these before writing your own version saves time and avoids reinventing well-tested code.

The random module generates pseudo-random values: random.randint(a, b) returns a whole number between a and b, including both ends. The math module adds functions and constants beyond the built-in arithmetic operators, like math.sqrt() and the constant math.pi.
Code Forge's Python runtime includes these modules just like a regular Python installation, so the same import statements you would use anywhere else work here too.
explanation.rule: Before writing a helper function from scratch, check whether the standard library already has one.

examples.title: Rolling a Die
examples.code:
import random

random.seed(7)
roll = random.randint(1, 6)
print(roll)
examples.note: randint(1, 6) returns a whole number from 1 to 6, both included — perfect for simulating a six-sided die. seed() is used here only so this example always prints the same result.

checks.question: What does random.randint(1, 6) return?
options: A whole number from 1 to 6, including both 1 and 6.
A whole number from 0 to 6, excluding 6.

feedback.correct: Correct — randint's range includes both endpoints.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. randint's second argument is included in the possible results, unlike range().

requirements: Use random.randint to pick the number.

hints: random.randint(1, sides) picks a whole number, both ends included.
Don't call random.seed() inside roll_dice — the harness seeds it for you before calling your function.
Return the number — don't print it inside roll_dice.
sides is the upper bound; 1 is always the lower bound.
